title: DNA, RNA & Protein Synthesis
description: DNA structure, Chargaff's rules, replication and repair, transcription, RNA processing, the genetic code, translation, mutations, gene regulation (operons, epigenetics) and core lab techniques such as PCR.

cards.title: How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C base pair together?
cards.body:
Three

A–T pairs have only **two**, so GC-rich DNA needs more heat to separate.

Each pair joins a purine (A, G) with a pyrimidine (C, T; U in RNA), which keeps the helix a uniform $2\,\mathrm{nm}$ wide. The two strands are antiparallel: they run $5'\to3'$ in opposite directions.

Key idea: more hydrogen bonds means a higher melting temperature.
cards.searchQuery: G-C base pair three hydrogen bonds DNA

cards.title: A double-stranded DNA sample is 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
cards.body:
$20\%$

**Chargaff's rules:** $A = T$ and $G = C$. If $A = 30\%$, then $T = 30\%$, leaving $40\%$ for $G + C$, so $G = 20\%$ and $C = 20\%$.

Watch out: the rules hold only for double-stranded DNA. Single-stranded DNA and RNA need not obey them.
cards.searchQuery: Chargaff's rules base percentages double-stranded DNA

cards.title: Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria on $^{15}\mathrm{N}$, then moved them to $^{14}\mathrm{N}$. Their results supported which model of DNA replication?
cards.body:
Semiconservative

Each new double helix has **one parental strand and one newly made strand**.

After one round in $^{14}\mathrm{N}$, all the DNA formed a single hybrid band, which ruled out the conservative model. After two rounds there were hybrid and light bands, which ruled out the dispersive model.

Key idea: a density gradient separated heavy, hybrid and light DNA.
cards.searchQuery: Meselson Stahl experiment semiconservative replication

cards.title: Which enzyme relieves the overwinding strain ahead of a replication fork by breaking, swiveling and rejoining DNA strands?
cards.body:
Topoisomerase

It cuts one or both strands, lets them swivel, then reseals them, so the helix ahead of the fork does not tighten.

Watch out: helicase is different. It unwinds the double helix at the fork, and single-strand binding proteins then keep the separated strands from re-pairing.
cards.searchQuery: topoisomerase relieves supercoiling replication fork

cards.title: DNA polymerase can't start a new strand from scratch. Which enzyme synthesizes the short RNA starter that it extends?
cards.body:
Primase

It makes an **RNA primer** (typically 5–10 nucleotides) whose free $3'$ end gives DNA polymerase a place to start.

Polymerases can only add nucleotides to an existing $3'$ end, so new DNA always grows $5'\to3'$. The leading strand needs one primer; the lagging strand needs one for each Okazaki fragment.
cards.searchQuery: primase RNA primer DNA replication

cards.title: On the lagging strand in E. coli, what do DNA pol III, DNA pol I and DNA ligase each do?
cards.body:
Pol III extends each primer into an Okazaki fragment; pol I replaces the RNA primers with DNA; ligase seals the nicks.

- **DNA pol III** extends each RNA primer into an Okazaki fragment.
- **DNA pol I** removes the RNA primer and fills the gap with DNA.
- **DNA ligase** joins the sugar-phosphate backbones of adjacent fragments.

Why: the strand is built in pieces because polymerase works only $5'\to3'$, which on this strand means moving away from the fork.
cards.searchQuery: lagging strand Okazaki fragments pol III pol I ligase

cards.title: Which enzyme lengthens the ends of linear chromosomes in germ cells, using an RNA template it carries with it?
cards.body:
Telomerase

When the RNA primer at the very end of a new strand is removed, there is no upstream $3'$ end for polymerase to extend, so chromosomes shorten each round.

**Telomeres** (repeats of $\text{TTAGGG}$ in humans) buffer this loss. Telomerase is active in germ cells and many cancer cells but not in most somatic cells.
cards.searchQuery: telomerase RNA template telomere lengthening germ cells

cards.title: An mRNA has the same sequence (with U in place of T) as which DNA strand?
cards.body:
The coding (nontemplate) strand

RNA polymerase reads the template strand $3'\to5'$ and builds a complementary RNA $5'\to3'$, so the RNA ends up matching the other strand.

Watch out: the template strand is complementary to the mRNA, not identical to it.
cards.searchQuery: coding strand versus template strand mRNA sequence

cards.title: In eukaryotic promoters, what sequence about 25 nucleotides upstream of the start point is a key binding site for transcription factors?
cards.body:
The TATA box

Transcription factors bind it first, then **RNA polymerase II** joins them to form the transcription initiation complex.

Key idea: unlike bacterial RNA polymerase, eukaryotic RNA polymerase can't recognize a promoter on its own.
cards.searchQuery: TATA box eukaryotic promoter transcription factors

cards.title: Name the three modifications that turn eukaryotic pre-mRNA into mature mRNA before it leaves the nucleus.
cards.body:
A $5'$ cap, a poly-A tail and splicing

- **$5'$ cap:** a modified guanine nucleotide.
- **Poly-A tail:** roughly 50–250 adenine nucleotides on the $3'$ end.
- **Splicing:** spliceosomes cut out introns and join the exons.

Why: the cap and tail help export the mRNA from the nucleus, protect it from hydrolytic enzymes and help ribosomes attach.
cards.searchQuery: pre-mRNA processing 5' cap poly-A tail splicing

cards.title: Which codon starts translation, and which three codons stop it?
cards.body:
Start: $\text{AUG}$. Stop: $\text{UAA}$, $\text{UAG}$, $\text{UGA}$.

$\text{AUG}$ also codes for methionine and sets the reading frame. The stop codons code for no amino acid; a release factor binds the stop codon in the A site and frees the polypeptide.

Mnemonic: U Are Away ($\text{UAA}$), U Are Gone ($\text{UAG}$), U Go Away ($\text{UGA}$).
cards.searchQuery: start codon AUG stop codons UAA UAG UGA

cards.title: An mRNA codon reads $5'$-GCA-$3'$. What is the matching tRNA anticodon, written $5'\to3'$? (letters only)
cards.body:
UGC

Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel: $5'$-GCA-$3'$ pairs with $3'$-CGU-$5'$, which reads $\text{UGC}$ when written $5'\to3'$.

Watch out: answering $\text{CGU}$ means you forgot to flip the strand. $\text{GCA}$ codes for alanine, so this tRNA carries Ala.
cards.searchQuery: codon anticodon pairing antiparallel tRNA 5' to 3'

cards.title: During elongation, what does each tRNA binding site on the ribosome (A, P and E) hold?
cards.body:
A: the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA. P: the tRNA holding the growing chain. E: the empty tRNA about to exit.

The polypeptide is transferred onto the A-site amino acid (rRNA catalyzes the peptide bond). The ribosome then shifts one codon, so tRNAs move A, then P, then E.

Mnemonic: **A**rrive, **P**olypeptide, **E**xit.
cards.searchQuery: ribosome A P E sites tRNA elongation translation

cards.title: Inserting or deleting nucleotides in a number that isn't a multiple of three causes what type of mutation?
cards.body:
A frameshift mutation

Every codon after the change is misread, usually giving a nonfunctional protein, often cut short by an early stop codon.

Example: substitution types are silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid, as in sickle-cell disease) and nonsense (codon becomes a stop).
cards.searchQuery: frameshift mutation insertion deletion not multiple of three

cards.title: What is the natural inducer of the lac operon, the molecule that binds and inactivates the lac repressor?
cards.body:
Allolactose

It is an isomer of lactose. Watch out: it isn't lactose itself, and IPTG is only a synthetic lab inducer.

The lac operon is **inducible**: usually off, because the repressor sits on the operator. When glucose is scarce, cAMP builds up and activates CAP, which helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter (positive control).
cards.searchQuery: lac operon allolactose inducer repressor

cards.title: How does abundant tryptophan switch off the trp operon in E. coli?
cards.body:
Tryptophan acts as a corepressor that activates the repressor.

The trp repressor is inactive on its own. When tryptophan binds it, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription.

Key idea: the trp operon is **repressible** (usually on; anabolic pathway), while the lac operon is inducible (usually off; catabolic pathway).
cards.searchQuery: trp operon tryptophan corepressor repressible operon

cards.title: What three components make up a single DNA nucleotide?
cards.body:
A phosphate group, deoxyribose (a five-carbon sugar) and a nitrogenous base

The base attaches to the sugar's $1'$ carbon and the phosphate to its $5'$ carbon.

Key idea: the sugar and phosphate form the backbone; the bases carry the information.
cards.searchQuery: DNA nucleotide components phosphate deoxyribose base

cards.title: Which two DNA bases are purines (double-ring bases)? Type their one-letter symbols.
cards.body:
A and G

**Purines** (adenine, guanine) have two fused rings. **Pyrimidines** (cytosine, thymine, and uracil in RNA) have one ring.

Mnemonic: **Pur**e **A**s **G**old (purines are A and G); CUT the pyrimidines (C, U, T).
cards.searchQuery: purines adenine guanine versus pyrimidines DNA bases

cards.title: What type of covalent bond links adjacent nucleotides in a single DNA strand?
cards.body:
A phosphodiester bond

It joins the $3'$ hydroxyl of one sugar to the $5'$ phosphate of the next nucleotide, building the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Key idea: this gives each strand a $5'$ end (free phosphate) and a $3'$ end (free hydroxyl).
cards.searchQuery: phosphodiester bond DNA backbone 3' hydroxyl 5' phosphate

cards.title: To which end of a growing DNA strand does DNA polymerase add each new nucleotide: the $5'$ end or the $3'$ end?
cards.body:
The $3'$ end

The free $3'$ hydroxyl attacks the incoming nucleotide's phosphate, so the strand grows $5'\to3'$.

Why: this is why a primer with a free $3'$ end is required, and why the lagging strand is made in fragments.
cards.searchQuery: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to 3' end 5' to 3' synthesis

cards.title: Give three structural differences between RNA and DNA.
cards.body:
RNA has ribose (not deoxyribose), uracil (not thymine), and is usually single-stranded.

- **Sugar:** ribose has a $2'$ hydroxyl that deoxyribose lacks.
- **Base:** uracil replaces thymine and pairs with adenine.
- **Strands:** RNA is typically single-stranded.

Why: the extra $2'$ hydroxyl makes RNA more reactive and less stable than DNA.
cards.searchQuery: RNA versus DNA differences ribose uracil single-stranded

cards.title: In double-stranded DNA, 22% of the bases are cytosine. What percentage are adenine? (number only)
cards.body:
$28\%$

Chargaff: $G = C = 22\%$, so $G + C = 44\%$. The remaining $56\%$ is $A + T$, split equally, so $A = 28\%$.

Tip: start with the paired base, then subtract from $100\%$ and halve.
cards.searchQuery: Chargaff rule problem cytosine percent adenine percent

cards.title: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, which radioactive element labeled the phage DNA but not its protein coat?
cards.body:
Phosphorus ($^{32}\mathrm{P}$)

DNA contains phosphorus but almost no sulfur, while proteins contain sulfur ($^{35}\mathrm{S}$) but no phosphorus.

Key idea: $^{32}\mathrm{P}$ entered the bacteria and appeared in the progeny phages, showing that **DNA is the genetic material**.
cards.searchQuery: Hershey Chase experiment phosphorus-32 DNA labeled phage

cards.title: Griffith found that heat-killed virulent S bacteria could make live harmless R bacteria deadly to mice. What is this process called?
cards.body:
Transformation

A "transforming principle" (later shown by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty to be DNA) passed from dead S cells to live R cells and changed their phenotype.

Watch out: Griffith did not know the principle was DNA; he only showed a heritable substance existed.
cards.searchQuery: Griffith experiment transformation heat-killed S bacteria

cards.title: In B-form DNA, about how many base pairs make up one full turn of the double helix (nearest whole number)?
cards.body:
$10$

One turn is about $3.4\,\mathrm{nm}$ long, and the pairs are stacked $0.34\,\mathrm{nm}$ apart.

Key idea: the helix is $2\,\mathrm{nm}$ wide, with a major groove and a minor groove where proteins read the bases.
cards.searchQuery: B-DNA 10 base pairs per turn 3.4 nm helix

cards.title: DNA wraps around an octamer of which basic proteins to form a nucleosome?
cards.body:
Histones

Two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 form the core octamer. Histones are rich in positively charged lysine and arginine, which bind DNA's negatively charged phosphates.

Key idea: nucleosomes are the first level of DNA packing into chromatin, the "beads on a string".
cards.searchQuery: nucleosome histone octamer DNA packaging chromatin

cards.title: How does the number of replication origins differ between a typical bacterial chromosome and a eukaryotic chromosome?
cards.body:
Bacteria have one origin per chromosome; eukaryotic chromosomes have many.

A bacterial chromosome is circular and small enough to copy from a single origin. Long linear eukaryotic chromosomes use many origins at once, which speeds up S phase.

Key idea: origins are rich in A–T pairs, which separate more easily.
cards.searchQuery: origin of replication bacteria one eukaryotes many

cards.title: How many replication forks form at a single origin of replication?
cards.body:
$2$

The two forks move in opposite directions, so replication is **bidirectional**. The open region between them is the replication bubble.

Example: a circular bacterial chromosome copies until the two forks meet on the opposite side.
cards.searchQuery: replication bubble bidirectional two replication forks origin

cards.title: Which enzyme breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs to unwind the double helix at the replication fork?
cards.body:
Helicase

It uses ATP to move along the DNA and separate the two strands, creating the fork.

Watch out: helicase does not relieve the supercoiling ahead of the fork. That's topoisomerase's job.
cards.searchQuery: helicase unwinds DNA replication fork

cards.title: What is the job of single-strand binding proteins at the replication fork?
cards.body:
They coat the separated template strands and keep them from re-pairing or folding.

This holds the strands open so polymerase can read the template bases.

Key idea: they stabilize the single strands; they do not unwind DNA themselves.
cards.searchQuery: single-strand binding proteins replication fork function

cards.title: Why is one new strand at a replication fork made continuously (leading) and the other in pieces (lagging)?
cards.body:
Polymerase can only build $5'\to3'$, and the two template strands run antiparallel.

The leading strand is built toward the fork, so it can be synthesized in one piece. The lagging strand must be built away from the fork, so it is made in short **Okazaki fragments** as the fork opens up more template.

Example: a fork copying $1{,}000$ nucleotides of template makes one primer on the leading strand but many on the lagging strand.
cards.searchQuery: leading strand lagging strand continuous discontinuous synthesis

cards.title: About how long are Okazaki fragments in E. coli compared with those in eukaryotes?
cards.body:
E. coli: roughly $1{,}000$–$2{,}000$ nucleotides. Eukaryotes: roughly $100$–$200$ nucleotides.

Because eukaryotic fragments are shorter, a eukaryotic chromosome needs many more primers on its lagging strands.

Key idea: fragment length differs by organism, but the mechanism is the same.
cards.searchQuery: Okazaki fragment length bacteria versus eukaryotes

cards.title: How does DNA polymerase proofread as it copies DNA?
cards.body:
It backs up and removes a mismatched nucleotide with its $3'\to5'$ exonuclease activity, then adds the correct one.

Proofreading cuts the error rate from about $1$ in $10^5$ to about $1$ in $10^7$ nucleotides.

Key idea: the same enzyme both adds nucleotides ($5'\to3'$) and removes the wrong ones ($3'\to5'$).
cards.searchQuery: DNA polymerase proofreading 3' to 5' exonuclease

cards.title: What does mismatch repair do, and when does it act?
cards.body:
After replication, repair enzymes find mismatched base pairs, cut out the incorrect stretch of the new strand and fill it in using the old strand as the template.

Together with proofreading it lowers the final error rate to about $1$ in $10^{10}$ nucleotides.

Why: the cell needs a way to tell old from new strand (in bacteria, by methylation) so it fixes the copy, not the original.
cards.searchQuery: mismatch repair after replication error rate DNA

cards.title: Thymine dimers caused by UV light are fixed by which type of DNA repair?
cards.body:
Nucleotide excision repair

Nuclease enzymes cut out a short stretch of damaged strand, then DNA polymerase fills the gap and ligase seals it.

Example: people with xeroderma pigmentosum have defective excision repair and are extremely sensitive to UV light.
cards.searchQuery: nucleotide excision repair thymine dimers UV xeroderma pigmentosum

cards.title: Bacteria grown for many generations in $^{15}\mathrm{N}$ are moved to $^{14}\mathrm{N}$ and replicate their DNA 3 times. What fraction of the DNA molecules still contain any $^{15}\mathrm{N}$?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{4}$

Three rounds give $8$ double helices from the original one. The two parental $^{15}\mathrm{N}$ strands stay in $2$ hybrid molecules, and the other $6$ are all $^{14}\mathrm{N}$.

Watch out: the number of molecules containing $^{15}\mathrm{N}$ stays at $2$ while the total doubles. Only $2$ of $16$ strands ($\frac{1}{8}$) are heavy.
cards.searchQuery: Meselson Stahl third generation fraction hybrid DNA

cards.title: What does the sliding clamp do during DNA replication?
cards.body:
It holds DNA polymerase onto the template so the enzyme stays attached while it copies long stretches.

The clamp is a ring-shaped protein that encircles the DNA and slides along it.

Key idea: it boosts **processivity**, the number of nucleotides added before the polymerase lets go.
cards.searchQuery: sliding clamp processivity DNA polymerase III

cards.title: What are the two steps of the central dogma, and what does each one make?
cards.body:
Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template; translation makes a polypeptide from an mRNA.

$$\text{DNA} \xrightarrow{\text{transcription}} \text{RNA} \xrightarrow{\text{translation}} \text{protein}$$

Watch out: in eukaryotes transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm. Some viruses add reverse transcription (RNA to DNA).
cards.searchQuery: central dogma transcription translation DNA RNA protein

cards.title: In which direction does RNA polymerase build an RNA strand? Type it as 5' to 3' or 3' to 5'.
cards.body:
$5'\to3'$

It adds ribonucleotides to the $3'$ end of the growing RNA, reading the template strand $3'\to5'$.

Key idea: every nucleic acid polymerase builds $5'\to3'$.
cards.searchQuery: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA 5' to 3' reads template 3' to 5'

cards.title: Unlike DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase can start a new strand without what?
cards.body:
A primer

RNA polymerase starts chains **de novo** at the promoter, so no primase is needed for transcription.

Why: it only has to make short, replaceable copies, so it can tolerate more errors than DNA polymerase, and it has little proofreading.
cards.searchQuery: RNA polymerase does not need a primer transcription initiation

cards.title: What is the name of the DNA sequence where RNA polymerase binds and initiates transcription?
cards.body:
The promoter

It lies upstream of the gene and sets where transcription starts and which strand is the template.

Key idea: promoters are not transcribed; they are signals read by RNA polymerase and transcription factors.
cards.searchQuery: promoter DNA sequence RNA polymerase binding site

cards.title: In bacteria, which subunit lets RNA polymerase recognize and bind a promoter, and is released after initiation?
cards.body:
The sigma ($\sigma$) factor

Core RNA polymerase can transcribe but can't find promoters well; with $\sigma$ attached it forms the **holoenzyme** that binds the promoter.

Key idea: different $\sigma$ factors direct RNA polymerase to different sets of genes, for example during heat shock.
cards.searchQuery: sigma factor bacterial RNA polymerase promoter recognition

cards.title: What are the three stages of transcription, in order?
cards.body:
Initiation, elongation, termination

- **Initiation:** polymerase binds the promoter and unwinds DNA.
- **Elongation:** it builds RNA $5'\to3'$ as the DNA rewinds behind it.
- **Termination:** the RNA and polymerase are released.
cards.searchQuery: transcription stages initiation elongation termination

cards.title: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA?
cards.body:
RNA polymerase II

Pol I makes most rRNA and pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.

Tip: pol **II** makes mRNA, so it is the one that needs the TATA box and general transcription factors.
cards.searchQuery: RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA eukaryotes pol I pol III

cards.title: Promoters lie "upstream" of a gene. Upstream is toward which end of the coding strand: $5'$ or $3'$?
cards.body:
The $5'$ end

Upstream is toward the start of the transcript and downstream is toward the end, with positions upstream of the start point numbered negative (the TATA box is near $-25$).

Key idea: RNA and the coding strand run in the same direction, so "upstream" is the same for both.
cards.searchQuery: upstream downstream DNA 5' end coding strand promoter

cards.title: A template strand reads $3'$-TACGGT-$5'$. What is the mRNA sequence, written $5'\to3'$? (letters only)
cards.body:
AUGCCA

Pair each template base with its complement, using U in place of T: $\text{T}\to\text{A}$, $\text{A}\to\text{U}$, $\text{C}\to\text{G}$, $\text{G}\to\text{C}$, $\text{G}\to\text{C}$, $\text{T}\to\text{A}$. Written under the template this gives $\text{AUGCCA}$, already $5'\to3'$.

Watch out: if the template had been written $5'\to3'$, you would have to reverse the result.
cards.searchQuery: transcribe template strand to mRNA complementary sequence problem

cards.title: How does transcription end in bacteria compared with eukaryotic pol II genes?
cards.body:
Bacteria: a terminator sequence in the RNA signals release. Pol II: the transcript is cut after a polyadenylation signal ($\text{AAUAAA}$), and polymerase keeps going briefly before it dissociates.

The cut at the polyadenylation signal is where the poly-A tail is added.

Key idea: in eukaryotes the transcript is released by cleavage; in bacteria the terminator itself ends transcription.
cards.searchQuery: transcription termination bacteria terminator eukaryotes polyadenylation signal

cards.title: What are distant eukaryotic DNA control elements that bind activator proteins and boost transcription of a gene?
cards.body:
Enhancers

Activators bound to an enhancer bend the DNA and contact the transcription machinery at the promoter, even from thousands of nucleotides away.

Key idea: enhancers explain why one gene can be active in a liver cell but silent in a neuron: the activators present differ.
cards.searchQuery: enhancers activators distal control elements eukaryotic transcription

cards.title: During splicing, are introns or exons removed from the pre-mRNA?
cards.body:
Introns

Exons are joined into the mature mRNA; introns are cut out and degraded.

Mnemonic: **ex**ons are **ex**pressed; **in**trons stay **in** the nucleus.
cards.searchQuery: splicing introns removed exons joined pre-mRNA

cards.title: What is a spliceosome made of, and what does it do?
cards.body:
It is a complex of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) plus other proteins that cuts out introns and joins exons.

Each snRNP contains a small RNA that base-pairs with the intron's ends, so RNA helps the catalysis.

Key idea: introns are cut at splice sites near their $5'$ and $3'$ ends.
cards.searchQuery: spliceosome snRNPs intron splicing mechanism

cards.title: What is the process called by which one pre-mRNA is spliced into different mRNAs with different combinations of exons?
cards.body:
Alternative splicing

It lets one gene code for several related proteins, so the number of proteins in a human exceeds the roughly $20{,}000$ genes.

Example: different exon choices can make the same gene produce a membrane-bound or a secreted form of a protein.
cards.searchQuery: alternative splicing one gene multiple proteins exons

cards.title: What name is given to an RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst?
cards.body:
A ribozyme

Examples include the rRNA that forms peptide bonds in the ribosome and some self-splicing introns.

Key idea: ribozymes show that RNA can store information and catalyze reactions, which supports the RNA world hypothesis.
cards.searchQuery: ribozyme catalytic RNA rRNA peptide bond

cards.title: A pre-mRNA transcript is $1{,}500$ nucleotides long and contains two introns of $300$ and $200$ nucleotides. Ignoring the cap and tail, how long is the mature mRNA? (number only)
cards.body:
$1000$ nucleotides

Splicing removes both introns: $1{,}500 - 300 - 200 = 1{,}000$.

Watch out: the cap and poly-A tail add nucleotides afterward, so a real mature mRNA is slightly longer than this.
cards.searchQuery: splicing problem calculate mature mRNA length after introns removed

cards.title: Why can bacteria start translating an mRNA before transcription finishes, while eukaryotes cannot?
cards.body:
Bacteria have no nucleus, so ribosomes can attach to an mRNA while RNA polymerase is still making it.

In eukaryotes, transcription and processing occur in the nucleus, and the finished mRNA must be exported before translation.

Key idea: the nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation and leaves time for RNA processing.
cards.searchQuery: coupled transcription translation bacteria no nucleus eukaryotes

cards.title: What are the roles of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA in protein synthesis?
cards.body:
mRNA carries the code, tRNA brings amino acids, and rRNA is the main component of ribosomes.

- **mRNA:** a copy of a gene read in codons.
- **tRNA:** matches an anticodon to a codon and carries one amino acid.
- **rRNA:** makes up most of the ribosome and catalyzes peptide bond formation.
cards.searchQuery: mRNA tRNA rRNA roles protein synthesis

cards.title: Which enzyme, used by retroviruses such as HIV, makes DNA from an RNA template?
cards.body:
Reverse transcriptase

The viral RNA is copied into DNA that is then integrated into the host genome.

Example: biotechnologists use it to make cDNA from mRNA, a copy that has no introns.
cards.searchQuery: reverse transcriptase retrovirus RNA to DNA HIV cDNA

cards.title: How many nucleotides make up one codon?
cards.body:
$3$

With four bases, a triplet gives $4^3 = 64$ possible codons, more than enough for the $20$ amino acids. Doublets would give only $4^2 = 16$.

Key idea: mRNA is read in non-overlapping triplets from the start codon.
cards.searchQuery: codon three nucleotides triplet genetic code 64 codons

cards.title: Of the $64$ possible codons, how many specify an amino acid?
cards.body:
$61$

The other $3$ are the stop codons ($\text{UAA}$, $\text{UAG}$, $\text{UGA}$). The $61$ sense codons code for just $20$ amino acids.

Watch out: $\text{AUG}$ is counted among the $61$ because it codes for methionine as well as signaling the start.
cards.searchQuery: 61 sense codons 3 stop codons genetic code

cards.title: The genetic code lets several codons specify the same amino acid, but no codon specifies two. What term describes this feature?
cards.body:
Redundant (or degenerate)

The code is redundant but **not ambiguous**: each codon has exactly one meaning.

Example: $\text{GCU}$, $\text{GCC}$, $\text{GCA}$ and $\text{GCG}$ all code for alanine. Third-position changes are often silent.
cards.searchQuery: genetic code redundant degenerate not ambiguous codons

cards.title: Why can a bacterium translate a human gene to make human insulin?
cards.body:
The genetic code is nearly universal: almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids.

This shared code is strong evidence for common ancestry, and it is what makes genetic engineering possible.

Watch out: the cell must still be able to express the gene, so the human gene used for insulin is usually inserted as cDNA, with no introns, because bacteria cannot splice.
cards.searchQuery: genetic code universal bacteria human insulin gene

cards.title: A protein has $100$ amino acids. How many nucleotides are in the coding region of its mRNA, counting the stop codon? (number only)
cards.body:
$303$

Each amino acid needs one codon: $100 \times 3 = 300$ nucleotides. The stop codon adds $3$ more.

Watch out: the whole mRNA is longer still, because of the $5'$ and $3'$ untranslated regions and the poly-A tail.
cards.searchQuery: mRNA coding length 100 amino acids 303 nucleotides stop codon

cards.title: Translate $5'$-AUGUUUGGCUGGUAA-$3'$ using: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, UGG = Trp, UAA = stop. Give the peptide with three-letter codes, joined by hyphens.
cards.body:
Met-Phe-Gly-Trp

Read from the first $\text{AUG}$ in triplets: $\text{AUG}\,|\,\text{UUU}\,|\,\text{GGC}\,|\,\text{UGG}\,|\,\text{UAA}$. The last codon is a stop and adds nothing.

Tip: always mark the triplets with slashes before looking anything up.
cards.searchQuery: translate mRNA sequence to amino acids codon table problem

cards.title: Which enzymes attach each amino acid to its correct tRNA, using ATP?
cards.body:
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases

There is one for each amino acid, and each recognizes both its amino acid and its matching tRNA.

Key idea: these enzymes make the code work, because the ribosome only matches anticodon to codon and cannot check which amino acid the tRNA carries.
cards.searchQuery: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase attaches amino acid to tRNA

cards.title: What are the two functional ends of a tRNA molecule?
cards.body:
The anticodon loop pairs with an mRNA codon; the $3'$ end carries the amino acid.

A tRNA folds into an L-shape by internal base pairing, which is drawn flat as a cloverleaf. The amino acid attaches to the $3'$ end of the molecule.

Key idea: one end reads the code and the other end carries the amino acid.
cards.searchQuery: tRNA structure anticodon loop 3' acceptor end cloverleaf

cards.title: What term describes the relaxed base pairing between the third codon base and the first anticodon base, which lets one tRNA read more than one codon?
cards.body:
Wobble

Because of wobble, cells need fewer than $61$ different tRNAs.

Example: a $\text{U}$ in the first anticodon position can pair with either $\text{A}$ or $\text{G}$ in the third codon position.
cards.searchQuery: wobble base pairing third codon position tRNA

cards.title: What is the sedimentation coefficient of a complete eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome? (e.g., 70S)
cards.body:
80S

It is made of a $60\mathrm{S}$ large subunit and a $40\mathrm{S}$ small subunit. Bacterial ribosomes are $70\mathrm{S}$ ($50\mathrm{S}$ + $30\mathrm{S}$).

Watch out: Svedberg units depend on shape as well as mass, so the numbers do not add up.
cards.searchQuery: eukaryotic ribosome 80S 60S 40S subunits prokaryotic 70S

cards.title: Outline how translation initiation proceeds in a eukaryotic cell.
cards.body:
The small subunit with the initiator tRNA binds the $5'$ cap, scans to the first $\text{AUG}$, and then the large subunit joins.

1. The initiator tRNA (carrying Met) binds the small ribosomal subunit.
2. This complex attaches to the mRNA's $5'$ cap and scans downstream to the start codon.
3. The large subunit joins, with the initiator tRNA in the P site.

Key idea: initiation factors help each of these steps.
cards.searchQuery: eukaryotic translation initiation small subunit 5' cap scans AUG

cards.title: What bacterial mRNA sequence just upstream of the start codon base-pairs with the 16S rRNA of the small subunit?
cards.body:
The Shine–Dalgarno sequence

It is a purine-rich ribosome binding site that positions the ribosome so that the $\text{AUG}$ lands in the P site.

Watch out: bacteria use this site, while eukaryotes use the $5'$ cap and scanning.
cards.searchQuery: Shine-Dalgarno sequence bacterial ribosome binding site 16S rRNA

cards.title: In bacteria, which modified amino acid does the initiator tRNA carry?
cards.body:
N-formylmethionine (fMet)

Every new bacterial polypeptide starts with fMet, and the formyl group is often removed later.

Key idea: eukaryotic initiator tRNA carries ordinary methionine.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial initiator tRNA N-formylmethionine fMet

cards.title: In the ribosome, what molecule catalyzes the formation of the peptide bond?
cards.body:
rRNA

The peptidyl transferase activity belongs to rRNA in the large subunit, so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

Key idea: the ribosomal proteins mostly support the structure; the catalytic site is made of RNA.
cards.searchQuery: ribosome peptidyl transferase rRNA catalyzes peptide bond

cards.title: A polypeptide is built from which end to which? Name the end made first.
cards.body:
The N-terminus (the amino end)

The first amino acid keeps its free amino group, and each new one adds to the carboxyl end, so the chain grows from N toward C.

Key idea: the mRNA is read $5'\to3'$, so the codon order matches the N-to-C order of the protein.
cards.searchQuery: polypeptide synthesis N-terminus to C-terminus direction

cards.title: What are the three steps of each elongation cycle in translation?
cards.body:
Codon recognition, peptide bond formation, translocation

1. An aminoacyl-tRNA pairs with the codon in the A site.
2. The polypeptide is transferred to the A-site tRNA, forming a peptide bond.
3. The ribosome shifts one codon along the mRNA (translocation).

Why: GTP is used for steps 1 and 3 to keep the process accurate and moving.
cards.searchQuery: translation elongation cycle codon recognition peptide bond translocation

cards.title: What protein binds a stop codon in the A site and triggers release of the finished polypeptide?
cards.body:
A release factor

It adds a water molecule to the end of the chain instead of an amino acid, freeing the polypeptide from the last tRNA. The ribosome then comes apart.

Key idea: no tRNA matches a stop codon.
cards.searchQuery: release factor stop codon A site translation termination

cards.title: What is a group of ribosomes simultaneously translating one mRNA called?
cards.body:
A polyribosome (polysome)

Several ribosomes follow one another along the mRNA, each at a different stage, so many copies of the protein are made quickly.

Example: electron micrographs show them as beads on an mRNA thread.
cards.searchQuery: polyribosome polysome multiple ribosomes one mRNA

cards.title: What short sequence at the start of a polypeptide directs the ribosome to the endoplasmic reticulum?
cards.body:
The signal peptide

A signal recognition particle (SRP) binds it, pauses translation and brings the ribosome to the ER membrane, where the chain enters the ER as it is made.

Key idea: it decides whether a protein is made on free ribosomes or on the rough ER.
cards.searchQuery: signal peptide SRP rough ER ribosome targeting

cards.title: What proteins help newly made polypeptides fold into their correct three-dimensional shape?
cards.body:
Chaperones (chaperone proteins, including chaperonins)

They shield the polypeptide from improper interactions while it folds.

Example: heat-shock proteins are chaperones whose levels rise when heat causes proteins to misfold.
cards.searchQuery: molecular chaperones chaperonins protein folding

cards.title: Which level of protein structure is determined directly by the mRNA codon sequence?
cards.body:
Primary structure

This is the sequence of amino acids. Higher levels of folding follow from it and from the cell environment.

Example: changing one codon can change one amino acid and, as in sickle-cell hemoglobin, the whole protein's behavior.
cards.searchQuery: primary structure amino acid sequence determined by codons

cards.title: Sickle-cell disease comes from a single-nucleotide substitution in the $\beta$-globin gene. Which amino acid replaces which? (e.g., Ala to Gly)
cards.body:
Glutamic acid is replaced by valine (Glu to Val)

The mRNA codon changes from $\text{GAG}$ to $\text{GUG}$ at position $6$ of the chain.

Key idea: a polar, charged residue becomes a hydrophobic one, so hemoglobin molecules stick together when deoxygenated. It's a **missense** mutation.
cards.searchQuery: sickle cell glutamic acid to valine GAG GUG beta globin

cards.title: A mutation changes an mRNA codon from $\text{GAA}$ to $\text{GAG}$, and both code for glutamic acid. What type of point mutation is this?
cards.body:
Silent

The protein is unchanged, because of the redundancy of the genetic code.

Why: most silent mutations are in the third codon position, where the code is most redundant.
cards.searchQuery: silent mutation GAA GAG same amino acid

cards.title: A mutation changes an mRNA codon from $\text{GAU}$ (aspartic acid) to $\text{GUU}$ (valine). What type of point mutation is this?
cards.body:
Missense

A different amino acid is inserted. The effect ranges from none to severe, depending on where the change falls and how similar the two amino acids are.

Example: the sickle-cell mutation is a missense mutation.
cards.searchQuery: missense mutation GAU GUU amino acid change

cards.title: A mutation changes an mRNA codon from $\text{UGG}$ (tryptophan) to $\text{UGA}$. What type of point mutation is this?
cards.body:
Nonsense

A codon for an amino acid becomes a **stop codon**, so translation ends early and a shortened protein is made.

Watch out: the earlier in the gene it happens, the more likely the protein is nonfunctional.
cards.searchQuery: nonsense mutation UGG to UGA premature stop codon

cards.title: What happens to the protein if exactly three nucleotides are deleted from the middle of a coding sequence?
cards.body:
One amino acid is lost (or changed) but the reading frame is preserved, so the rest of the protein is unchanged.

If the deleted triplet is not aligned with a codon, the neighboring codons are altered, but the downstream frame is still preserved.

Example: the most common cystic fibrosis allele is a $3$-nucleotide deletion that removes one phenylalanine.
cards.searchQuery: in-frame deletion three nucleotides reading frame preserved

cards.title: Name two physical mutagens and the DNA damage each causes.
cards.body:
UV light causes thymine dimers; X-rays (ionizing radiation) cause strand breaks.

Chemical mutagens include base analogs and agents that alter bases, such as nitrous acid.

Why: damage that escapes repair becomes a permanent mutation when the cell replicates.
cards.searchQuery: mutagens UV thymine dimers X-rays strand breaks DNA damage

cards.title: Which kind of mutation can be passed to offspring: somatic or germline?
cards.body:
Germline

Mutations in cells that give rise to gametes can be inherited. **Somatic** mutations affect only the individual and its descendant cells, as in most cancers.

Key idea: only germline mutations contribute to evolution of the species.
cards.searchQuery: germline mutation inherited versus somatic mutation

cards.title: What are segments of DNA that can move from one location in the genome to another called?
cards.body:
Transposable elements (transposons)

They can disrupt genes or regulatory regions when they insert, so they are a source of mutations.

Example: Barbara McClintock discovered them in maize kernels.
cards.searchQuery: transposons transposable elements jumping genes McClintock

cards.title: Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded run of which trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene?
cards.body:
CAG

The repeat codes for a stretch of glutamine, and a long repeat gives a toxic protein.

Key idea: repeat expansions are mutations that can grow from one generation to the next, so symptoms often begin earlier in later generations.
cards.searchQuery: Huntington disease CAG repeat expansion HTT gene

cards.title: What is a cluster of related genes in bacteria that share one promoter and are switched on or off together?
cards.body:
An operon

It is transcribed as a single mRNA, so all of its genes are expressed together.

Key idea: an operon has a promoter, an operator and the structural genes.
cards.searchQuery: operon definition promoter operator genes bacteria

cards.title: What is the name of the DNA segment, between the promoter and the genes of an operon, to which a repressor binds?
cards.body:
The operator

When the repressor is bound, RNA polymerase is physically blocked and transcription stops.

Watch out: do not confuse the **operator** (a DNA site) with the **repressor** (a protein) or the promoter (the RNA polymerase site).
cards.searchQuery: operator DNA segment repressor binding site operon

cards.title: What does the lac repressor do when lactose is absent?
cards.body:
It binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase, so the lac genes are off.

The repressor protein is always made from the separate regulatory gene $lacI$. When allolactose is present it binds the repressor and changes its shape so it can't bind the operator.

Key idea: lactose acts as an **inducer**, switching the operon on.
cards.searchQuery: lac repressor binds operator absence of lactose

cards.title: In E. coli, when both glucose and lactose are present, is the lac operon transcribed at a high or low level?
cards.body:
Low

Lactose inactivates the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP isn't activated and RNA polymerase binds the promoter poorly.

Tip: high expression needs two things: **no repressor** on the operator (lactose present) and **active CAP** (glucose absent).
cards.searchQuery: lac operon glucose and lactose present low transcription CAP cAMP

cards.title: Which structural gene of the lac operon codes for $\beta$-galactosidase, the enzyme that splits lactose?
cards.body:
$lacZ$

$lacY$ codes for permease, which brings lactose into the cell, and $lacA$ for a transacetylase.

Key idea: $\beta$-galactosidase cuts lactose into glucose and galactose, and also makes allolactose.
cards.searchQuery: lacZ gene beta-galactosidase lac operon lacY permease

cards.title: When glucose is scarce, which small molecule accumulates and binds CAP (catabolite activator protein) to increase lac transcription?
cards.body:
cAMP

The cAMP-CAP complex binds near the promoter and helps RNA polymerase bind it.

Key idea: this is **positive control**, and it ensures the cell uses glucose before switching to lactose.
cards.searchQuery: cAMP CAP catabolite activator protein lac operon glucose

cards.title: Does adding acetyl groups to histone tails generally increase or decrease transcription of nearby genes?
cards.body:
Increase

Acetylation removes the positive charge on lysine, so histones grip DNA less tightly, chromatin opens, and transcription proteins reach the promoter.

Key idea: this is an **epigenetic** change, since the DNA sequence itself is unchanged.
cards.searchQuery: histone acetylation loosens chromatin increases transcription

cards.title: Does methylation of cytosines in a eukaryotic promoter generally repress or activate the gene?
cards.body:
Represses

Methyl groups on cytosine recruit proteins that compact chromatin, so the gene is silenced.

Example: genomic imprinting and X inactivation involve long-term silencing by DNA methylation.
cards.searchQuery: DNA methylation cytosine promoter gene silencing

cards.title: What are small noncoding RNAs of about 22 nucleotides that bind complementary mRNAs and block their translation or cause degradation?
cards.body:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs)

Each one is bound by a protein complex that guides it to mRNAs with a complementary sequence.

Key idea: this is **RNA interference**, a way of controlling gene expression after transcription.
cards.searchQuery: microRNA miRNA gene silencing RNA interference mRNA

cards.title: What name is given to highly condensed chromatin that is generally not transcribed?
cards.body:
Heterochromatin

Loosely packed chromatin that is available for transcription is **euchromatin**.

Example: in female mammals, one X chromosome is condensed into heterochromatin (a Barr body).
cards.searchQuery: heterochromatin condensed transcriptionally inactive euchromatin

cards.title: Which bacterial enzymes cut DNA at specific short sequences, often palindromic, and are used to make recombinant DNA?
cards.body:
Restriction enzymes (restriction endonucleases)

Many cut so that they leave single-stranded "sticky ends", which can pair with any DNA cut by the same enzyme. DNA ligase then joins them.

Example: EcoRI cuts at $5'$-GAATTC-$3'$.
cards.searchQuery: restriction enzymes cut DNA palindromic sequence sticky ends EcoRI

cards.title: What are the three steps in each PCR cycle, in order?
cards.body:
Denaturation, annealing, extension

1. **Denaturation** (about $95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$): heat separates the DNA strands.
2. **Annealing** (about $50$–$65\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$): primers pair with the template.
3. **Extension** (about $72\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$): a heat-stable polymerase such as Taq extends the primers.
cards.searchQuery: PCR steps denaturation annealing extension Taq polymerase

cards.title: Ideal PCR doubles the number of double-stranded DNA molecules each cycle. Starting from one molecule, how many exist after 5 cycles? (number only)
cards.body:
$32$

The number of molecules is $2^n$, and $2^5 = 32$.

Watch out: the formula assumes perfect efficiency, and real reactions level off as primers and nucleotides run out. Fragments of exactly the target length first appear in cycle $3$.
cards.searchQuery: PCR amplification 2 to the n copies after cycles

cards.title: What name is given to proteins that bind specific DNA sequences or each other to help RNA polymerase II begin transcription?
cards.body:
Transcription factors

General transcription factors assemble at the promoter, while **activators** and repressors bind enhancers or other control elements to turn a gene up or down.

Key idea: the set of transcription factors present in a cell largely decides which genes are expressed.
cards.searchQuery: transcription factors RNA polymerase II promoter activators
